newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil mum on CVRD selloff details.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil mum on CVRD selloff details.

text.p: Brazil on Wednesday dashed market hopes it would set an asking share price in the upcoming privatization of Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD), but answered critcism of the sale.

Planning Minister Antonio Kandir said the asking price for the block sale of 40-45 percent of the mining giant's voting shares would be announced one day before the publication of tender details relating to that sale.
Shares in CVRD fell 1.54 percent after surging on speculation the government would finalize details of what is to become South America's biggest privatization.

National Development Bank (BNDES) privatization director Jose Pio Borges told reporters the tender details would be published at the end of February or early in March and the block sale would "probably" take place 45 days after that.

The government hopes to raise more than $5.0 billion by privatizing its 51 percent stake in CVRD's total capital, first through the block sale and then via sales to staff and sales on international stock markets.

Kandir and Borges said they had found an answer to critics who accuse the government of selling off untold mineral wealth lying undetected in two neighboring areas of the Amazonian state of Para which are controlled by CVRD.
Opponents of the privatization have seized on reports of massive but undefined gold, copper and other mineral deposits in Carajas and Serra do Leste to demand the sale be stopped.
They argue that the government's plan to issue existing CVRD shareholders, including itself, with debentures exchangeable for future mineral finds might leave Brazil shortchanged.

Under a proposal drawn up by CVRD and approved by the National Privatization Council, CVRD and the BNDES will jointly invest 300 million reais over the next five years to carry out research, principally in the two areas. Rights to mineral wealth found would be split 50-50 between the company and the bank.

Whoever buys CVRD will assume its stake in the exploration venture and may also buy the BNDES' stake should it choose to sell it. BNDES may also opt to jointly develop any finds at Carajas and Serra do Leste or buy the rights from CVRD's new owners and develop the areas through independent contractors.
"This plan will end criticism that Vale does not know how to put a value on its mineral wealth," CVRD president Francisco Schettino told reporters.
BNDES director Pio Borges said the debentures plan would apply to areas where studies showed that mineral deposits that would become profitable 30 years or more after the sale of CVRD.
The debentures would entitle shareholders to between one and 2.5 percent of the value of future discoveries.
The value of areas where CVRD is currently producing would be included in the asking price of shares to be sold at privatization, Pio Borges said.

Planning Minister Kandir said the new plan for Carajas and Serra do Leste wiped out the risk of the government setting its debenture charge too low to reap the rewards of future finds and too high for CVRD's owners to feel inclined to invest in them.
